analysis.one_liner: Exempted offshore drilling permit applicants who met new federal safety rules from the Gulf drilling moratorium.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote; it had 1 sponsor and 8 cosponsors, all Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: After the BP Deepwater Horizon disaster, the Interior Department paused offshore drilling and permitting while new safety rules took hold. This bill would have carved companies back out of that pause: any drilling applicant that had met two federal safety notices and passed required inspections would be exempt from the moratorium, and the Interior Secretary would have to decide on the permit within 30 days. It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies that wanted to resume drilling and permitting immediately, plus Gulf Coast energy workers and service businesses whose work stopped during the moratorium.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have exempted any drilling permit applicant from the Interior Department's July 2010 offshore moratorium if the applicant complied with the two 2010 safety notices to leaseholders and completed all required safety inspections [S2][S3].
Once the Secretary determined an applicant was in compliance, the department would have been required to decide whether to issue the permit within 30 days, preventing an indefinite wait [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the safety and environmental risk of resuming offshore drilling faster than the moratorium allowed, at a time when the cause of the BP blowout was still under investigation; coastal fishing and tourism economies would absorb any repeat accident.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have overridden a safety suspension for any applicant that met two specific notices and inspections, even though compliance with those notices is not the same as proving a well can be drilled safely; it substituted a checklist for the Interior Department's broader judgment [S3].

The hard 30-day deadline for a permit decision would have forced the agency to act on drilling permits on a fixed clock regardless of how complex or unresolved the safety questions were for a given application [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine cost of the moratorium was real: it idled rigs and Gulf energy jobs. But the bill's remedy was blunt. It would have let companies back to work on the strength of paperwork compliance rather than a finding that drilling could be done safely, and it put the permitting agency on a 30-day deadline. An honest supporter would acknowledge that it traded certainty of speed for certainty of safety review, and the record here shows the bill never received a hearing or a vote, so it was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on July 19-20, 2010, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Olson introduced the bill on July 19, 2010, in the middle of the federal moratorium imposed after the BP Deepwater Horizon spill [S1][S5].
Eight Republican colleagues cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].

The bill was referred to the Natural Resources Committee on July 19 and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on July 20, 2010, and the record shows no markup, hearing, floor action, or vote at any point afterward [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill expired in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Interior Department kept full discretion over the moratorium and the pace of permitting, and the safety pause stayed in place rather than being shortened by statute. Gulf drilling opponents came out ahead; Gulf energy workers who wanted rigs running again did not.

for.name: Rep. Pete Olson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to limit the offshore drilling moratorium [S1][S3].

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 19, 2010, and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters (the sponsor and eight cosponsors) were Republicans, and no Democrat supported the bill on the record; because the bill never reached a vote, there are no roll-call numbers to show where the full chamber stood.

industries.note: The bill would have let compliant companies resume drilling and permitting months earlier than the moratorium allowed, restoring suspended revenue. The cost fell on the public in the form of safety and spill risk that the moratorium, issued right after the BP Deepwater Horizon disaster, was meant to manage.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast energy service and rig workers
industries.note: A faster end to the moratorium would have returned offshore work and pay to Gulf communities where the drilling pause idled rigs and service jobs. Their interest here ran alongside the drillers' interest, and the bill's death left them waiting on the slower administrative path.
These industries benefit from a lower risk of another spill. Because the bill never passed, the safety pause ran its course and their exposure was not shortened.
